title: Schelling on New York
hook: Measure a random mix on New York's outline. What can the number tell you, and what not?

knows: the Schelling mechanism from the Economics lesson (a simple moving rule sorts a grid), though this card explains its own squares and rule
that cities can have neighbourhoods where one group is concentrated
doesNotKnow: that a segregation index depends on the size of the unit it is measured on (a random mix already scores about 0.4 to 0.5 on small blocks)
what a model like this can and cannot say about a real city

misconception: If a simple model reproduces a city's pattern, then that is why the city looks that way. Second: a mix placed at random would score a segregation index near zero.
objective: The learner can explain that an unevenness index such as D depends on the unit it is measured on (a random mix scores about 0.45 on 2 x 2-cell blocks and less on larger ones, and a census tract holds thousands of people), that in this toy model a simple moving rule sorts the grid to about 0.75, and that the model leaves out money, prices, jobs, history and who was allowed to live where, so it does not show why any real city looks as it does.

claims.text: The index of dissimilarity D measures how unevenly two groups are spread over a set of units, from 0 (both groups spread in the same proportions over every unit) to 1 (no unit holds both groups); it equals the share of one group that would have to change units for an even spread. On the card only as 'how unevenly spread (0 even, 1 fully apart)'; the 'would have to change units' gloss is in this claim only (cultural review R4).
claims.source: Massey, D. S. and Denton, N. A. (1988). The dimensions of residential segregation. Social Forces 67(2): 281-315 (evenness, index of dissimilarity). Computed in engine.ts dissimilarity(): D = 0.5 * sum over aligned k x k blocks of |a_i/A - b_i/B|, over agents only (walls and empty cells ignored). Builder: citation from memory, not opened (no egress). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14: VERIFIED. Citation (Social Forces 67(2): 281-315, 1988; evenness as one of five dimensions, indices surveyed per dimension) confirmed from search-indexed bibliographic and abstract listings only; the paper itself was not opened (publisher unreachable). Definition, endpoints and the 'would have to change units' gloss confirmed by derivation from the formula: 0 iff a_i/A = b_i/B in every unit, 1 iff no unit holds both; because the signed terms sum to 0, the positive part equals D, the share of one group to move for an even spread. engine.ts dissimilarity() re-implemented independently, same values. See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md.

claims.text: In this model, two equal groups placed at random on the grid already score about 0.4 to 0.5 in 2 x 2 boxes of cells, before anyone moves.
claims.source: engine.ts run(seed, 30), frames[0], dissimilarity(frame, 40, 2). check.mjs (2026-10-14): the lesson's seeds (1 to 50 without 3 and 36, 48 seeds) start at 0.42-0.53, mean 0.46; mix 1 (seed 1, the default) 0.47, mix 2 0.44. Seed 1 is simply the first seed, not chosen for its result; seeds 3 and 36 are left out of New mix because their settled frame leaves one region of the city more than 90% one group (edge artefact, cultural review R2), not for their D. Same rule as the brief's check script (check.mjs shows start frames, end frames and ticks identical for seeds 1 to 50). v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, spec company/design/specs/schelling-on-new-york-v3.md section 11): the question says 'the 2 x 2 boxes drawn on it (a segregation index: 0 even, 1 fully apart)'; the stage readout 'mix N' is the seed; the reveal quotes the start value of the learner's own pinned mix P (spec section 7), which is on the reveal stage's caption. Reset to unverified (wording).

claims.text: In this model, at the 30% setting (move if fewer than 30% of occupied neighbouring cells hold the same group), the grid settles with nobody moving, and D in 2 x 2 boxes rises to about 0.75.
claims.source: engine.ts run(seed, 30). check.mjs (2026-10-14), the lesson's 48 seeds: settled D in 2 x 2 boxes 0.67-0.83, mean 0.75; all settle in 7-24 ticks; mix 1 (seed 1): 0.47 -> 0.76 in 7 rounds; mix 2: 0.44 -> 0.76 in 12 (matches the brief's real-mask numbers, company/domains/briefs/checks/nyc-mask-40.md). v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, spec company/design/specs/schelling-on-new-york-v3.md section 11): the slider is removed (design review D5) and the setting is fixed at 30%, the old cap (cultural review 2, ruling (a)); the rule is a static line, 'Move if fewer than 30% of neighbours are like them'. The readout is 'Round' (was Tick) and 'would move N%' (was 'would stay'), N = ceil(100 x movers / agents) at the frame shown, so it reads 0% only when nobody would move; check.mjs asserts that no frame of any lesson seed at 30% reads 0% with movers > 0, and that no region (at least 10 agents) is over 90% one group at any round at 30% (worst 0.86). Reset to unverified.

claims.text: D depends on the box size it is measured in: the same model grid scores less in larger boxes; at the random start about 0.46 in 2 x 2, 0.26 in 4 x 4 and 0.14 in 8 x 8 boxes, and settled at 30% about 0.75, 0.53 and 0.33.
claims.source: engine.ts dissimilarity(frame, 40, k) for k = 2, 4, 8 over the lesson's 48 seeds (check.mjs, 2026-10-14): start 0.42-0.53 (mean 0.46) / 0.21-0.31 (0.26) / 0.10-0.19 (0.14); settled at 30% 0.67-0.83 (0.75) / 0.44-0.64 (0.53) / 0.22-0.45 (0.33). Mix 1: start 0.47 / 0.27 / 0.12, settled 0.76 / 0.53 / 0.34. Mix 2: start 0.44 / 0.24 / 0.14, settled 0.76 / 0.54 / 0.31. Single cells (1 x 1) score 1.00 (every cell holds at most one household); this stays in the source only, the card no longer has a 1 x 1 chip (spec section 3). v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, spec company/design/specs/schelling-on-new-york-v3.md section 11): on the stage each box chip the learner has pressed shows its value at the start and now; the reveal quotes the start value of the pinned mix P in the largest box size other than 2 x 2 that the learner looked at on P (k*), and that value is on the reveal stage's caption. Reset to unverified (text).

claims.text: In this model, a simple moving rule sorts the grid: a simplified version of Thomas Schelling's segregation model.
claims.source: Simulation as in c6. Model: Schelling, T. C. (1971). Dynamic models of segregation. Journal of Mathematical Sociology 1(2): 143-186 (verified as a citation in economics.mild-preferences-sharp-divides.c6; the stage rule is the same simplified variant, moving to a random empty cell). Reworded per cultural review R3: 'a simple moving rule', not 'preferences'. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14: VERIFIED. Simulation as c6 (the sorting itself reproduces). Schelling 1971 citation rests on economics.mild-preferences-sharp-divides.c6 (verified 2026-10-14, secondary records). engine.ts reproduces abm.ts frame for frame on an all-land mask (check.mjs), so 'simplified version' carries over. See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md.

claims.text: This model does not show why any real city looks as it does.
claims.source: Judgement about the model's scope (cultural review R3, brief claim 9): the rule has no money, prices, jobs, history or rules about who may live where (see c14), both groups follow the same rule and may move anywhere, and the grid is not a map of people (c12). Shown in the reveal, in the same paragraph as the model's result. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14: VERIFIED (scope judgement). Read engine.ts: inputs are only mask, empty share, two equal groups, seed and threshold; agents move to any empty cell at no cost. A model with none of the causes listed in c14 cannot show why a real city looks as it does. The card's wording ('does not show') stays within that. See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md.

claims.text: Late-1930s US government maps graded neighbourhoods in US cities for lending risk.
claims.source: Mapping Inequality: Redlining in New Deal America, University of Richmond Digital Scholarship Lab, https://dsl.richmond.edu/panorama/redlining/ (the Home Owners' Loan Corporation maps, security grades A-D). Its area-description data (github.com/americanpanorama/HOLC_Area_Description_Data) date most surveys 1937-1939; New York City's map is 1938, so the card says 'late-1930s'. On the card, inside the sentence that begins 'In US cities': 'late-1930s government maps grading neighbourhoods for lending risk'. No acronym, no neighbourhood named beside a grade (R7). v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): split from v1 c10a into c10a (this, Mapping Inequality only), c10d (Aaronson et al. 2021) and c10e (Fishback et al. 2024), one source each, after the fact-check dispute; '1938' changed to 'late-1930s'. Builder: Mapping Inequality site not opened (no egress). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (v2): VERIFIED. Read the Mapping Inequality data (github.com/americanpanorama): A-D grades, 'Best' to 'Hazardous', with mortgage fields; most surveys dated 1937-1939. The site itself was unreachable. That the Home Owners' Loan Corporation was a federal agency comes from search-indexed descriptions only (Mapping Inequality overview, ICPSR). See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md (pass 2).

claims.text: The maps' grades are associated with later outcomes in the graded neighbourhoods, such as home values and home ownership.
claims.source: Aaronson, D., Hartley, D. and Mazumder, B. (2021). The effects of the 1930s HOLC 'redlining' maps. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 13(4): 355-392 (later home ownership, house values, rents and segregation by grade). The authors argue for an effect; the card states only an association, which understates the source. The card says outcomes, not lending: on the card 'The grades are associated with later home values and ownership'. v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): split from v1 c10a after the fact-check dispute ('lending' was the authors' inferred mechanism, not a measured outcome). Builder: paper not opened (no egress). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (v2): VERIFIED from the search-indexed abstract only; the paper was not opened. The abstract reports lower later home ownership, house values and rents in lower-graded areas. 'Associated with' claims less than the authors do, which is acceptable. See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md (pass 2).

claims.text: Research is mixed on whether the maps caused these later differences or recorded lending practice that already existed.
claims.source: Fishback, P., Rose, J., Snowden, K. and Storrs, T. (2024). New Evidence on Redlining by Federal Housing Programs in the 1930s. Journal of Urban Economics 141: 103462 (NBER Working Paper w29244, 2021): exclusion of such neighbourhoods by federal programmes predates the maps, and the maps had little effect on lending; set against Aaronson et al. (c10d), which finds an effect. On the card: 'research is mixed on whether the maps caused this or recorded earlier practice'. v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): split from v1 c10a after the fact-check dispute (the 'mixed' clause needs its own source). Builder: paper not opened (no egress); the date is 2024 (journal) / 2021 (NBER), not 2022 as in R7. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (v2): VERIFIED from search-indexed abstracts only; the paper was not opened. Fishback et al. find that the FHA's exclusion of these neighbourhoods came before the maps and that the maps had little effect on lending. Set against Aaronson et al. (c10d), this supports 'research is mixed'. Fishback et al. study lending, not later home values, so the disagreement is about cause. See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md (pass 2).

claims.text: In US cities, housing and lending discrimination by race widened wealth gaps between groups, largely through home equity.
claims.source: Rothstein, R. (2017). The Color of Law: A Forgotten History of How Our Government Segregated America. New York: Liveright (federal, state and local housing and lending discrimination by race; its effect on home equity and so on wealth). On the card, the words 'housing and lending discrimination by race, widening wealth gaps' inside 'In US cities, households did not all have the same choices: the documented history includes housing and lending discrimination by race, widening wealth gaps, and late-1930s government maps ...'. v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, spec company/design/specs/schelling-on-new-york-v3.md section 11): split per spec section 12: this claim is narrowed to the housing-discrimination and wealth-gap words; 'households did not all have the same choices' and 'lending discrimination' in the late-1930s grades are carried by c10f. 'by race' added to the card per cultural review 2, pass 4, ruling 6.1, and the claim text moves with the phrase. The card's 'widening' claims slightly less than 'widened' (earlier fact-check note). Builder: book not opened (no egress). STILL NEEDS A PAGE for the home-equity and wealth argument; per cultural pass 3, if none is found, replace the source, not the order.

claims.text: In US cities, households did not all have the same choices: in many of the area descriptions behind the late-1930s government lending-risk grades, residents' race is recorded among the reasons for a neighbourhood's grade.
claims.source: Mapping Inequality, University of Richmond Digital Scholarship Lab: HOLC area-description data, github.com/americanpanorama/HOLC_Area_Description_Data (ad_data.json, about 7,930 forms, including New York City forms). The forms record residents' race in their own fields and name it among the reasons for a grade, in fields such as detrimental_influences, infiltration_of and clarifying_remarks. The forms use the period's own racial terms; this note describes them and does not quote them (cultural review 2, pass 4, ruling 6.3). No neighbourhood is named here or on the card (R7). On the card: 'households did not all have the same choices' and 'lending discrimination by race' in the sentence that begins 'In US cities'. v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, spec company/design/specs/schelling-on-new-york-v3.md section 11): new claim, split from c10b per spec section 12; 'in many area descriptions' rather than every form or grade (cultural pass 4, ruling 6.2), and stated as what the forms recorded, not as an inference about what lenders did. Builder: data not opened by me; the spec author's keyword search is a scope check, not a verification. Fact-checker: verify from the forms and give field names and a count.

claims.text: Income and wealth differences between groups are part of the documented history of where households live.
claims.source: NYU Furman Center, State of New York City's Housing and Neighborhoods (annual report), https://furmancenter.org/stateofthecity (income differences across New York City neighbourhoods and groups). Builder: not opened (no egress). The card names income after discrimination and does not present it as a separate neutral cause (R3). Fact-checker: confirm the report covers income by group, or name a better single source. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14: DISPUTED. The named source cannot carry the text. Per search-indexed listings (furmancenter.org unreachable), the Furman Center State of the City citywide tables give New York City median household income by race and ethnicity (present-day). They do not cover wealth, and they are not a 'documented history of where households live'. Also, the card has no separate sentence for this claim: its only income/wealth words are 'then income and wealth gaps it widened', which c10b carries. Fix (builder): either withdraw c10c and let c10b carry 'income and wealth gaps', or keep it as an income-only claim ('income differs between groups in New York City') sourced to a named Furman Center edition and table, and source wealth separately (e.g. the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances). See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md. | WITHDRAWN 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, v2): per the fact-check, the Furman Center tables are present-day NYC income by group, not a documented history, and do not cover wealth. The card no longer has an income clause; the only remaining wealth words ('widening wealth gaps') are carried by c10b (Rothstein 2017). No learner-visible text depends on this claim.

claims.text: The grid's shape comes from New York City's official city boundaries, rasterised to 40 x 40 cells of about 1.2 km (576 land cells).
claims.source: NYC Department of City Planning, Borough Boundaries, BYTES of the BIG APPLE release 16A (2016), nybb.shp, EPSG:2263; obtained from the PyPI wheel geopandas-0.14.4-py3-none-any.whl (geopandas/datasets/nybb_16a.zip, sha256 b4a98fc3b77be5af58676de9560c2782b902b83d1d8c7914dea8d0e75177e2a1), downloaded 2026-10-14 because the NYC Open Data host was unreachable; rasterised by company/domains/briefs/checks/nyc-mask-rasterise.mjs (cell centres, even-odd point-in-polygon, cell 3,855 ft); output company/domains/briefs/checks/nyc-mask-40.json, documented in nyc-mask-40.md. The lesson inlines only the 200-byte land bitmask (engine.ts MASK_HEX); no region labels reach the lesson (R2). check.mjs confirms MASK_HEX equals the JSON's land cells. v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): claim text says 'city boundaries' (cultural review 2, advisory); the dataset is still the DCP Borough Boundaries file named above. Text change only; reset to unverified for re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (v2): VERIFIED. engine.ts is unchanged since pass 1, when the mask was re-derived from the DCP file (576 land cells, cells 3,855 ft, about 1.18 km). The outline of the five borough boundaries is the city boundary, so 'city boundaries' is accurate. See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md (pass 2).

claims.text: A toy model on a grid shaped like New York City: each A or B mark stands for one household in a made-up model; two made-up equal groups; not New York's people and not a cause. The 30% setting is a setting in this model, not a measure of anyone.
claims.source: Judgement about the model (cultural review R9, R1, R6). On the stage: S1 'Made-up model: each [A] A or [B] B is one household. Not New York's people.' in the map's empty top-left water corner (and above the pair at the reveal), and S3 'A setting, not a measure of anyone.' directly above the static rule line. The map's and the pair's alt text say 'made-up households'. Density is equal everywhere in the model (one household per land cell, 10% empty) while real density varies. v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, spec company/design/specs/schelling-on-new-york-v3.md section 11): S1 reworded per spec section 4 (cultural pass 4, ruling 2: GO). Reset to unverified.

claims.text: In this model, a random mix scores about 0.4 to 0.5 in 2 x 2 boxes of the grid (at most 4 households each): chance alone leaves many boxes holding only one group, and the same mix scores lower in larger boxes. So a segregation number depends on its unit and means little without it.
claims.source: Recall card (R10). Restates c5, c7 and c17 (48 lesson seeds: start 0.42-0.53 in 2 x 2, about 0.26 in 4 x 4, 0.14 in 8 x 8; at the start 34-47% of 2 x 2 boxes hold only one group). A 2 x 2 box holds at most 4 land cells, each with at most one household. One range, 0.4 to 0.5, in the question and here. Carries no real-city figure and no group names. v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, spec company/design/specs/schelling-on-new-york-v3.md section 11): 'boxes' and 'at most 4 households each' (spec section 9 proposal), 'one group' (cultural pass 4, ruling 2). The learning designer owns the recall and is asked to confirm. Reset to unverified.

claims.text: Not modelled: money, prices, history, who was allowed to live where.
claims.source: Scope of the rule (engine.ts): the only inputs are the city mask, the share of empty cells, the two equal groups, the seed and the threshold; any household may move to any empty cell at no cost, and no rule bars anyone (it is the absence of such rules that is not modelled, so 'was allowed' is accurate as a statement of what is left out). v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, spec company/design/specs/schelling-on-new-york-v3.md section 11): the line is S4, inside the map's top-left water corner, shown once the grid has moved (round > 0 on any mix) and kept after Reset and New mix (cultural pass 4, ruling 5.3); at the reveal it sits under the pair. 'jobs' dropped and 'could' -> 'was allowed to' (spec section 4; cultural pass 4, rulings 2 and 3). The reveal no longer repeats the list. Reset to unverified.

claims.text: A census tract holds thousands of people. A 2 x 2 box in this grid holds at most 4 households.
claims.source: Tract size: US Census Bureau, Glossary, 'Census Tract' (https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/about/glossary.html), which gives tracts generally between 1,200 and 8,000 people, optimum about 4,000 (builder: from memory, not opened). Grid box: derivation, a 2 x 2 box holds at most 4 cells, each with at most one household. On the card: 'Mix N began at D in 2×2 boxes (at most 4 households each); ... a census tract holds thousands of people.' The comparison is in people, never in area (spec section 3). v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, spec company/design/specs/schelling-on-new-york-v3.md section 11): 'block' -> 'box', 'squares' -> 'households'. Reset to unverified (text).

claims.text: In this model, random mixes run under the same rule settle into clumps in different places: on the cells both settled grids fill, two mixes hold the same group about half the time.
claims.source: engine.ts run(seed, 30), last frames of two seeds compared cell by cell over cells that hold a household in both. check.mjs (2026-10-14): consecutive lesson seeds (each seed with the next in the New mix order, 48 pairs) agree on 0.41-0.59 of shared cells, mean 0.51; mix 1 vs mix 2: 229 of 463 cells (0.49); mix 2 vs mix 4: 231 of 464 (0.50). On the card: 'The rule sorted your mixes into clumps in different places', and the reveal stage pins the learner's own two settled mixes (P and Q) side by side, same size, same rule, identical neutral frames. v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, spec company/design/specs/schelling-on-new-york-v3.md section 11): new claim (spec sections 2 and 11).

claims.text: In this model, chance alone leaves many small boxes one group: at the random start, 34-47% (mean 39%) of the 2 x 2 boxes that hold a household hold only one group, against 3-16% of 4 x 4 and 0-11% of 8 x 8 boxes; settled at 30%, 64-81% of 2 x 2 boxes.
claims.source: engine.ts frames, aligned k x k boxes over the 40 x 40 grid; a box counts if it holds at least one household and is one-group if all its households are in one group (a box with one household counts). check.mjs (2026-10-14), the 48 lesson seeds: start 2 x 2 34-47% (mean 39%), 4 x 4 3-16% (11%), 8 x 8 0-11% (2%); settled at 30%: 2 x 2 64-81% (72%). Mix 1: start 72/181 (40%), settled 135/180 (75%). Mix 2: start 65/184 (35%), settled 127/181 (70%); 4 x 4 start 7/58 (12%); 8 x 8 start 0/18 (0%). On the card: the readout 'one-group boxes N%' (start -> now once the grid has moved), a neutral square outline on each one-group box in explore (never on the reveal pair), and the reveal's 'Each holds at most 4 households; chance alone left N% one group' with N from the learner's pinned mix P. v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, spec company/design/specs/schelling-on-new-york-v3.md section 11): new claim (spec sections 3 and 11); 'one-group' for 'one-colour' (cultural pass 4, ruling 2).

recall.question: In this model, a random mix scores about 0.4 to 0.5 in 2 × 2 boxes of the grid (at most 4 households each). What does that tell you about a segregation number?
options: It depends on the unit it is measured on, so the unit must be stated
The random mix is already half sorted before anyone has moved
The number is broken, so it should not be used at all
recall.why: A 2 × 2 box holds at most 4 households, so chance alone leaves many boxes holding only one group. The same mix scores lower in larger boxes. A number without its unit says little.
